text: Is antivirus or EDR installed and running on all devices?
why: Unprotected devices let ransomware run without being blocked or flagged.
fix: Deploy antivirus or EDR to every laptop, desktop and server, and check coverage monthly.

text: Is multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled for email, VPN and admin accounts?
why: Stolen passwords are a common way in. MFA stops most logins made with them.
fix: Turn on MFA for email, remote access and every admin account first, then for all users.

text: Are operating systems and software patched at least monthly?
why: Ransomware groups exploit known, already-fixed vulnerabilities in unpatched systems.
fix: Set a monthly patch cycle and patch internet-facing systems within days of critical updates.

text: Do normal users have admin rights on their own computers?
why: Malware runs with the user's rights. Admin rights let it disable defences and spread.
fix: Remove local admin rights from everyday accounts and use separate admin accounts when needed.

text: Is incoming email filtered for phishing and malicious attachments?
why: Phishing email is one of the most common ways ransomware gets delivered.
fix: Enable phishing and attachment filtering on your mail service and block risky file types.

text: Is suspicious activity on devices and accounts monitored?
why: Attackers often spend days inside a network before encrypting. Monitoring can catch them first.
fix: Turn on alerts in your EDR or security tools and name a person who responds to them.

text: Are logs from key systems collected in one central place?
why: Attackers delete local logs. Central logs let you see what happened and when.
fix: Send logs from servers, firewalls and identity systems to a central log store and keep 90 days.

text: Do you get alerts for unusual file changes, such as many files renamed or encrypted?
why: Mass file changes are an early sign that encryption has started.
fix: Enable file activity or ransomware-behaviour alerts in your EDR or file server.

text: Are security logs reviewed at least weekly?
why: Logs nobody reads do not help you spot an intrusion in time.
fix: Book a weekly slot to review security alerts and failed or unusual logins.

text: Do staff know how to report a suspected phishing email?
why: Staff are often the first to see an attack. A quick report shortens the response time.
fix: Publish one simple way to report phishing, such as a report button or a shared address.

text: Are important systems and data backed up regularly?
why: Without backups, the only ways back are paying the ransom or losing the data.
fix: Back up critical data at least daily and servers at least weekly.

text: Is at least one backup kept offline or immutable?
why: Ransomware often encrypts or deletes backups it can reach.
fix: Keep one backup copy offline or on immutable storage.

text: Have you tested restoring from backup in the last six months?
why: Untested backups often fail or turn out incomplete when you need them.
fix: Restore a sample of files and one full system from backup every quarter and record the result.

text: Is there a written list of critical systems in the order they must be restored?
why: During an outage, time is lost deciding what to bring back first.
fix: List critical systems, their owners and their restore order, and keep a printed copy.

text: Is there an agreed recovery time target for critical systems?
why: Without a target, you cannot tell whether your backups can restore fast enough.
fix: Agree how many hours each critical system can be down and check your restore tests meet it.

text: Is there a written incident response plan that covers ransomware?
why: Without a plan, people improvise under pressure and make mistakes.
fix: Write a short ransomware response plan covering roles, first steps, communication and recovery.

text: Do staff know the first steps to take if they see a ransom note?
why: Quick, correct first steps, such as disconnecting the device, limit how far it spreads.
fix: Give all staff a one-page guide: disconnect from the network, do not power off, call IT.

text: Have you run a ransomware drill or tabletop exercise in the last year?
why: Drills show the gaps in a plan before a real attack does.
fix: Run a one-hour tabletop exercise once a year using a ransomware scenario.

text: Is there an up-to-date list of emergency contacts, including IT, management and outside help?
why: Email and chat may be down during an attack, so contact details must exist elsewhere.
fix: Keep an offline contact list with IT, leadership, your insurer and incident response partners.

text: Is there a way to quickly isolate infected machines from the network?
why: Ransomware spreads across the network. Fast isolation limits the damage.
fix: Set up network isolation in your EDR or switches and document who can trigger it.
